reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD
clinicalPearls: Also known as hepatic veno-occlusive disease, it is a form of hepatic sinusoidal injury classically seen after haematopoietic stem cell transplantation and high-dose myeloablative conditioning
The classic clinical triad is tender hepatomegaly, weight gain with fluid retention, and jaundice developing in the weeks after transplantation
Other important causes include certain chemotherapeutic agents, radiation, and ingestion of pyrrolizidine alkaloids in some herbal preparations
The syndrome represents non-thrombotic post-sinusoidal outflow obstruction, so it produces portal hypertension with ascites
Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by criteria such as the Baltimore and modified Seattle definitions, with Doppler ultrasound showing features like reversed portal flow
Severe disease can progress to multi-organ failure and carries high mortality, making early recognition after transplant critical
Risk is increased by pre-existing liver disease, intensive conditioning regimens, and certain drug exposures, so prevention and vigilance in high-risk patients matter
Management includes supportive care with careful fluid and sodium balance, and defibrotide is used for severe disease; transjugular liver biopsy with pressure measurement may aid uncertain cases
reference.pathophysiology: Sinusoidal obstruction syndrome begins with toxic injury to the endothelial cells lining the hepatic sinusoids and the small central (terminal hepatic) venules, typically from conditioning chemoradiotherapy, certain cytotoxic drugs, or pyrrolizidine alkaloids. Damaged endothelium detaches and, together with cellular debris and deposited fibrin, embolises downstream to obstruct sinusoidal and post-sinusoidal blood flow. The resulting outflow block causes sinusoidal congestion, centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis, and subsequent fibrous narrowing of the small venules. Because obstruction is at the sinusoidal and post-sinusoidal level rather than in the large hepatic veins, the picture is one of tender congestive hepatomegaly, fluid retention, jaundice, and portal hypertension, which in severe cases extends to renal and pulmonary dysfunction and multi-organ failure.
additionalDifferentials: Budd-Chiari syndrome (large hepatic vein or IVC obstruction)
Congestive hepatopathy from right heart failure
Fungal or other infective hepatic infiltration in the immunocompromised
additionalInvestigations: Doppler ultrasound of the liver assessing hepatic and portal venous flow, including reversal of portal flow
Serial liver biochemistry, bilirubin, and monitoring of weight and fluid balance
Application of established clinical diagnostic criteria in the post-transplant setting
Transjugular liver biopsy with hepatic venous pressure gradient measurement in diagnostic uncertainty
Assessment of renal and pulmonary function to gauge severity and multi-organ involvement
Review of conditioning regimen and drug exposures
redFlags: Rapidly rising bilirubin with worsening hepatomegaly and fluid retention after haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, signalling severe disease
Progression to renal impairment, pulmonary dysfunction, or multi-organ failure
Refractory ascites and rapid weight gain
Encephalopathy or coagulopathy indicating hepatic failure
reference.prognosis: Mild disease often resolves with supportive care, but severe sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, particularly when accompanied by multi-organ failure after transplantation, carries a high mortality; early recognition, risk reduction, and timely use of defibrotide in severe cases improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Failing to consider the diagnosis when jaundice and fluid retention develop after stem cell transplantation
Confusing it with Budd-Chiari syndrome, which involves large-vessel obstruction and differs in management
Aggressive fluid loading that worsens congestion and ascites
Overlooking non-transplant causes such as pyrrolizidine alkaloid-containing herbal remedies
